title: DATEDIFF on a Column Blocks the Seek
description: DATEDIFF on a date column is non-sargable and scans; rewrite the condition as a plain date range to seek. Why it matters: date-math predicates are everywhere in reporting, and this is one of the most common ways they silently become non-sargable.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About
This lesson is another variation on the "don't wrap the column" theme, this time with date math. Using `DATEDIFF()` around a date column to check "was this within the last 7 days?" feels natural to write, but it silently breaks the database's ability to use an index on that column.

Why does this happen? `DATEDIFF(DAY, OrderDate, '2026-01-01')` computes a brand-new number — "how many days between this row's date and today" — for every row, on the fly. That computed number doesn't exist anywhere in the index; the index only stores the original `OrderDate` values. So to check "is this computed difference between 0 and 6," SQL Server has to calculate it fresh for every single row, which means visiting every row — exactly the scan you were trying to avoid.

Picture a librarian sorted every book by its exact publication date, but a visitor asks "find me every book published within 7 days of today" by having the librarian calculate the exact day-difference for each book one at a time. That calculation step, repeated per book, means checking the whole shelf instead of jumping to the right section. The fix is to flip the math: instead of computing a difference from every row, compute the two boundary dates once (`today` and `today - 7`), and compare the raw `OrderDate` column against those fixed boundaries — a simple range check the index can seek straight to.

## Scenario
A dashboard shows orders from the **last 7 days**. The developer wrote the filter with `DATEDIFF`:

```sql
WHERE DATEDIFF(DAY, OrderDate, '2026-01-01') BETWEEN 0 AND 6
```

There is a perfectly good index on `OrderDate`, yet the query scans the whole table.

## Why it's slow
Wrapping the column in `DATEDIFF(...)` (or `DATEADD`, `YEAR`, `MONTH`, ...) produces a **computed value**. SQL Server can only seek on the *bare* indexed column, so it must evaluate the function for **every row** — an **Index Scan** — before it can filter.

> Note: `CAST(OrderDate AS DATE)` is a special case the optimizer *can* still seek. But `DATEDIFF`/`DATEADD` around the column are **not** sargable.

## The fix
Express the same window as a **half-open range** on the raw column:

```sql
WHERE OrderDate >= '2025-12-26' AND OrderDate < '2026-01-02'
```

Now the index can **seek** straight to the matching rows.

## What to look for
- Bad: an **Index Scan** on `IX_Orders_OrderDate` reading all 200k rows.
- Good: an **Index Seek** with a tiny fraction of the logical reads.
startingQuery: SELECT OrderId, CustomerId, OrderDate, Total FROM Orders WHERE DATEDIFF(DAY, OrderDate, '2026-01-01') BETWEEN 0 AND 6;
hints: The operator reading Orders is a Scan, not a Seek. Why can't the OrderDate index seek?
DATEDIFF(DAY, OrderDate, ...) wraps the column in a function, so the range is hidden from the index.
Rewrite as a half-open range on the bare column: WHERE OrderDate >= '2025-12-26' AND OrderDate < '2026-01-02'.
